items.title: How to prevent leaks from Claude Code's 'Don't ask again' file
items.summary: This guide details how to find and remove secrets that were inadvertently committed to projects and repositories hosted on GitLab. We’ve confirmed that GitLab’s own infrastructure secrets are protected.In Claude Code, Anthropic’s coding agent, a developer can approve a shell command by selecting “Yes, and don’t ask again.” Claude then saves that exact command to .claude/settings.local.json in the project folder and runs it without asking in the future. If the command contained a password or a token, so does the file:{  "permissions": {    "allow": [      "Bash(npm test:*)",      "Bash(curl --header \"PRIVATE-TOKEN: glpat-EXAMPLEdummyTOKEN1234\" \"https://gitlab.com/api/v4/projects/1234567/issues?state=closed\")",    ]  }}Claude Code keeps the file out of Git through the developer's personal global excludes, not through the project's .gitignore. That protection lives on one laptop and does not travel with the repository, so the file gets committed and pushed wherever the repository lives. In early November 2026, Apiiro reported that this issue resulted in 104,185 copies of the file to appear in public repositories, 1,122 of them holding at least one secret. Hundreds more secrets were only in history, in files that had since been deleted.If your developers use Claude Code with repositories hosted on GitLab, this guide shows how to prevent this from happening moving forward, assess exposure now or in the past, and clean every affected project up at once.Prevent: Keep the file out of your repoThere are a few actions you can perform to ensure a developer cannot commit the file by accident, and that if one slips through, you hear about it. There are four layers you can put in place, each a little more work than the last, and the order below is a reasonable one to follow. All of them are settings a group owner changes once; this is the one part of the process GitLab Duo can walk you through but cannot do for you, since its access to GitLab settings is read-only.Start with .gitignoreThe simplest fix is also the one Claude Code should have done for you but does not: a line in each repository's .gitignore that reads .claude/settings.local.json. Claude Code only ever adds the exclusion to the developer's own global git configuration, which stays on that laptop.If you're on Premium or Ultimate, put the same line into the .gitignore in your group's file templates project (in the group, go to Settings > General > Templates), so that every project created from now on inherits it without anyone having to remember.Block the file name with a push rule (Premium and Ultimate)A push rule turns the convention into something GitLab enforces. In the group, go to Settings > Repository > Pre-defined push rules and, under Prohibited filenames, enter:(^|/)\.claude/settings\.local\.json$From then on, any push that tries to add that file, in the root of the repository or in any subdirectory, on any branch, is rejected before it lands, and the developer sees a message naming the pattern.There are two things to know about how push rules behave, both of which matter here. The rule only checks files being added, not changes to a file that is already tracked, which is why cleaning up the existing copies has to come first. And a rule set on the group is copied into projects created after that moment; it does not reach back to projects that already exist. For those, you set the same rule on each project, either from the project's own Settings > Repository > Push rules page or, if you have more than a handful, with a loop over the group's project ids:POST /api/v4/projects/<id>/push_rule   {"file_name_regex": "(^|/)\\.claude/settings\\.local\\.json$"}For a project that already has push rules of its own, use PUT on the same path instead; POST will answer 422 Project push rule exists.Add Secret Push Protection for the tokens (Ultimate)The push rule stops the file by name. Secret Push Protection looks at the content of every push, whatever the file is called, and rejects it if it finds a known token format. On GitLab Self-Managed and Dedicated, you first allow the feature for the instance under Admin > Settings > Security and compliance; on GitLab.com, that part is already done. Then you turn it on for each project under Secure > Security configuration > Secret push protection, or for a whole group at once through the group security settings API.Scan everything with one policy (Ultimate)A scan execution policy on the top-level group runs GitLab Secret Detection in every project, including ones that have no .gitlab-ci.yml at all, and individual projects can't switch it off. Create it under Group > Secure > Policies > New policy > Scan execution policy, with one rule that runs on every pipeline and a second that runs on a weekly schedule. The scheduled run looks through history the first time it runs; add the variable SECRET_DETECTION_HISTORIC_SCAN: 'true' to that rule if you want every weekly run to cover full history rather than only new commits.
